questions.q: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because:
questions.solution:
When phenol loses its proton the resulting **phenoxide** ion has its negative charge delocalised into the benzene ring over three carbons, which stabilises it considerably.

An ethoxide ion has no such delocalisation — the charge sits entirely on the oxygen.

A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid: phenol is about $\text{p}K_a\ 10$ against ethanol's $16$, a difference of a million times.

Electron-withdrawing groups on the ring stabilise the anion further, which is why 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid) is a genuinely strong acid.

questions.q: Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition because:
options: Ketones have two electron-releasing alkyl groups and more steric hindrance
questions.solution:
Two effects work in the same direction.

**Electronic:** a ketone has **two** alkyl groups releasing electron density ($+\text{I}$) into the carbonyl carbon, reducing its partial positive charge and so its attraction for a nucleophile. An aldehyde has only one.

**Steric:** two alkyl groups also crowd the carbon more, hindering the nucleophile's approach.

So reactivity runs $\text{HCHO} > \text{RCHO} > \text{RCOR}'$, with formaldehyde the most reactive of all since it has no alkyl group at all.

questions.q: In **aqueous** solution, the order of basicity of methylamines is:
questions.solution:
In water the observed order is $\mathbf{2^\circ > 1^\circ > 3^\circ}$, which is not what the inductive effect alone would predict.

Three factors compete:

**$+\text{I}$ effect** — more alkyl groups push more electron density onto nitrogen, favouring $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ$.

**Solvation** — the protonated ion is stabilised by hydrogen bonding to water, and more alkyl groups leave fewer N-H bonds to hydrogen bond with, favouring $1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ$.

**Steric hindrance** — bulky groups obstruct protonation, penalising $3^\circ$.

The compromise puts secondary first. **In the gas phase, with no solvent, the order is the pure inductive one:** $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ$ — which is the cleanest possible demonstration that solvation is what causes the anomaly.

Chlorine is electronegative and withdraws electron density through the sigma bonds ($-\text{I}$ effect), which **disperses** the negative charge on the carboxylate ion and stabilises it.

More chlorines means more stabilisation and a stronger acid:

$\text{Cl}_3\text{CCOOH} > \text{Cl}_2\text{CHCOOH} > \text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH} > \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$

Trichloroacetic acid has $\text{p}K_a\ 0.7$ against acetic acid's $4.76$ — about ten thousand times stronger.

The inductive effect falls off sharply with distance, so a chlorine three carbons away has almost no effect.

questions.q: The bond linking two amino acids in a protein is:
questions.solution:
A **peptide bond** is an amide linkage, $-\text{CO}-\text{NH}-$, formed by condensation between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, with the loss of water.

It has partial double-bond character from resonance, which makes it **planar and rigid** — and that rigidity is what makes defined protein secondary structures such as the alpha helix possible.

A glycosidic bond joins sugars, an ester bond appears in fats, and a phosphodiester bond links nucleotides in DNA.

questions.q: Aryl halides such as chlorobenzene are much less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution than alkyl halides because:
options: The C-Cl bond has partial double-bond character from resonance
questions.solution:
A lone pair on the chlorine is delocalised into the ring, giving the **C-Cl bond partial double-bond character**. It is therefore shorter and stronger and much harder to break.

The $sp^{2}$ carbon is also more electronegative than an $sp^{3}$ one, holding the bond more tightly, and the ring's pi cloud repels an approaching nucleophile.

Substitution is possible but needs forcing conditions, such as $623\ \text{K}$ and $300\ \text{atm}$ for the Dow process — or strong electron-withdrawing groups ortho and para to the halogen, which is why 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene reacts readily.

questions.q: Which compound will **not** give the iodoform test?
questions.solution:
The iodoform test is positive for a **methyl ketone** ($\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$) or an alcohol oxidisable to one ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}-$).

Ethanal is $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$ ✓, propanone is $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ ✓, ethanol is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ ✓.

**Propanal** is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ — the carbon next to the carbonyl is a $\text{CH}_2$, not a $\text{CH}_3$, so there is no methyl ketone group and the test is **negative**.

This is the standard way of telling propanal from propanone.

questions.q: Amino acids exist in solution mainly as:
questions.solution:
An amino acid has both an acidic $-\text{COOH}$ and a basic $-\text{NH}_2$ group, so an internal proton transfer occurs, giving a **zwitterion**: $\text{H}_3\text{N}^{+}-\text{CHR}-\text{COO}^{-}$.

The molecule carries both charges and is electrically neutral overall.

This explains properties that would otherwise be puzzling for small organic molecules: high melting points, solubility in water rather than organic solvents, and behaviour like an ionic solid.

The pH at which the zwitterion concentration is greatest, and the molecule does not migrate in an electric field, is the **isoelectric point**.

questions.q: Oxidation of a secondary alcohol gives:
questions.solution:
A secondary alcohol has one hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, so oxidation gives a **ketone** — and stops there, since further oxidation would require breaking a C-C bond.

A **primary** alcohol goes to an aldehyde and then on to a carboxylic acid, which is why a mild reagent such as PCC is needed to stop at the aldehyde.

A **tertiary** alcohol has no hydrogen on that carbon and resists oxidation altogether under ordinary conditions.

questions.q: How many amino acids are commonly found in proteins?
questions.solution:
**20** standard amino acids are encoded by the genetic code and make up essentially all proteins.

Of these, nine are **essential** in humans — they cannot be synthesised by the body and must come from the diet.

questions.q: How many carbon atoms are there in acetic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$?
questions.solution:
One carbon in the methyl group and one in the carboxyl group: $\mathbf{2}$ carbon atoms.

Its molecular formula is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$, with a molar mass of $60\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

questions.q: A tripeptide is formed from three amino acids. How many molecules of water are released?
questions.solution:
Each peptide bond is formed by a condensation releasing one water molecule.

Three amino acids in a chain need $3 - 1 = \mathbf{2}$ peptide bonds, so **2** water molecules are released.

In general, a polypeptide of $n$ residues releases $(n-1)$ waters.

questions.q: How many alpha hydrogens does propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$, have?
questions.solution:
The alpha carbons are the two methyl carbons flanking the carbonyl, and each carries three hydrogens.

$2 \times 3 = \mathbf{6}$ alpha hydrogens.

These are the acidic hydrogens that make aldol condensation and the iodoform reaction possible.

questions.q: Glucose has the molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$. How many chiral carbon atoms does the open-chain form contain?
questions.solution:
Open-chain glucose is an aldohexose: C1 is the aldehyde, C6 is a $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, and C2 to C5 each bear four different groups.

So there are $\mathbf{4}$ chiral carbons, giving $2^{4} = 16$ stereoisomers of which glucose is one.

On cyclisation C1 becomes chiral too, which is what creates the alpha and beta anomers.

questions.q: Explain why the basicity of aliphatic amines in aqueous solution follows the order $2^\circ > 1^\circ > 3^\circ$, while in the gas phase it follows $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ$. Also explain why aromatic amines such as aniline are far weaker bases than aliphatic ones.
questions.solution:
**What basicity depends on.** An amine is basic because the lone pair on nitrogen accepts a proton. Anything that makes that lone pair more available, or makes the resulting ammonium ion more stable, increases basicity.

**The gas phase first, because it is the simpler case.**

With no solvent, only the **inductive effect** operates. Each alkyl group releases electron density ($+\text{I}$) onto the nitrogen, making the lone pair more available and stabilising the positive charge on the protonated ion.

More alkyl groups therefore means more basic:

$3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > \text{NH}_3$

This is the order actually measured in the gas phase, and it is exactly what the inductive effect predicts on its own.

**In water, two further factors appear.**

**Solvation.** The protonated amine $\text{R}_n\text{NH}_{(4-n)}^{+}$ is stabilised by **hydrogen bonding** to surrounding water molecules, and that stabilisation needs **N-H bonds** to donate from. Count them:

$1^\circ$ ammonium $\text{RNH}_3^{+}$: three N-H bonds

$2^\circ$ ammonium $\text{R}_2\text{NH}_2^{+}$: two

$3^\circ$ ammonium $\text{R}_3\text{NH}^{+}$: one

So solvation favours exactly the **opposite** order: $1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ$.

**Steric hindrance.** Three bulky alkyl groups physically obstruct the approach of a proton and of solvating water molecules, penalising $3^\circ$ specifically.

**The compromise.** Going from $1^\circ$ to $2^\circ$, the gain from the added $+\text{I}$ effect outweighs the loss of one hydrogen bond, so basicity rises. Going from $2^\circ$ to $3^\circ$, the loss of solvation plus the steric penalty outweighs the further inductive gain, so basicity falls.

The result is $\mathbf{2^\circ > 1^\circ > 3^\circ}$.

**Why the two orders differ is itself the evidence.** The gas-phase order is the pure inductive prediction; the aqueous order deviates from it. Since the only thing added is the solvent, **solvation must be the cause** of the deviation. This is about as clean a controlled experiment as physical organic chemistry offers.

**Aromatic amines.** Aniline, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$, has $\text{p}K_b \approx 9.4$ against methylamine's $3.4$ — roughly a million times less basic.

The reason is **resonance**. The nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, spreading onto the ortho and para carbons. That lone pair is therefore **not fully available** to accept a proton.

Protonating it would also **destroy** that delocalisation and lose the stabilisation it provides, so the anilinium ion is relatively unstable. The $-\text{I}$ effect of the $sp^{2}$ ring carbon pulls in the same direction.

Substituents confirm the mechanism: electron-**withdrawing** groups such as $-\text{NO}_2$ pull the lone pair away even further and make aniline weaker still, while electron-**releasing** groups such as $-\text{CH}_3$ make it slightly stronger. That the effect tracks the ring's electron density so predictably is what shows resonance into the ring is responsible.
